603.title: Entertaining angels (Hebrews 13:1–2)
603.howItsDone: Many Catholic parishes, religious houses and charities practice hospitality to strangers, from welcoming newcomers at Mass to meals and shelter for travelers and the homeless, and Benedictine monasteries still receive guests as Christ, following the Rule of Saint Benedict.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the long list of the faithful in Hebrews eleven. Your line was faith is the substance. Whose name did you add to the list? Day six hundred three.

The hottest part of the day. An old man sits at the door of his tent, under the oaks of Mamre, and looks up to see three strangers standing nearby. He doesn't wait to find out who they are. He runs to meet them, bows to the ground, and has bread baked and a calf prepared, while they rest in the shade. That's Abraham in Genesis eighteen, and by the end of the visit it's clear these were no ordinary travelers. Centuries later, the letter to the Hebrews is nearly finished. The big arguments are over. And in its last chapter, among a few short pieces of advice, the writer reaches back for that afternoon.
screen: `THREE STRANGERS AT MAMRE.` → `ABRAHAM RUNS TO MEET THEM.` → `HEBREWS REMEMBERS THAT AFTERNOON.`

segments.voice: Chapter thirteen begins with two kinds of love, side by side. First, love for the family of believers. Then love for people you don't know at all. The Douay-Rheims puts it this way: "And hospitality do not forget; for by this some, being not aware of it, have entertained angels." The King James Bible, which many English speakers grew up with, gave us the phrase that stuck: angels unawares. The Greek word behind hospitality is philoxenia, which is simply love of strangers. Not love of guests you invited. Love of the person you didn't expect. Hebrews names no one here, but its first readers would have thought of stories they knew. Abraham at Mamre, feeding three visitors. Lot, taking two strangers into his house in Sodom. And Catholic Bibles hold another one, in the book of Tobias: a young man sets out on a long journey with a hired companion who calls himself Azarias, and only at the very end does the companion reveal that he is the angel Raphael. A whole road trip, and nobody knew. Notice what Hebrews doesn't say. It doesn't promise that every stranger is an angel, or tell you to be kind in case one is. The point runs the other way: you can't sort people in advance, so welcome everyone. Jesus says it even more directly in Matthew twenty-five: "I was a stranger, and you took me in." Saint Benedict wrote it into his rule for monks: every guest who comes to the door is to be received as Christ himself.
screen: `PHILOXENIA: LOVE OF STRANGERS.` · `ABRAHAM, LOT, TOBIAS AND RAPHAEL.` · `YOU CAN'T SORT PEOPLE IN ADVANCE.` · `I WAS A STRANGER, AND YOU TOOK ME IN.` · then, large: `ANGELS UNAWARES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: welcome a stranger, starting in your mind. Settle, and breathe slowly. Bring to mind someone you passed recently without really seeing: the person who bagged your groceries, a new face at work or at church, a neighbor whose name you never learned. Picture their face as clearly as you can. Now picture yourself greeting them properly, by name if you know it, with a moment more attention than usual. Let that feel ordinary. If you pray, you can hold the line, I was a stranger, and you took me in, and ask to notice the next stranger. If you don't, just hold the face kindly. The bell holds the time.
Entertaining angels. Hebrews thirteen: welcome strangers, because some, without knowing it, have welcomed angels. Today's word.
Your line: angels unawares. Today, welcome one stranger properly: learn a name, hold a door, make room at a table, say hello first. Day six hundred three.

it says some have welcomed angels without knowing. the point is to welcome everyone.
in the book of Tobias, the angel Raphael travels in disguise
he calls himself Azarias and reveals who he is only at the end.
the Greek word for hospitality means love of strangers
philoxenia: not guests you invited, but people you didn't expect.

fork.setup: you're Abraham, sitting at your tent door in the heat of the day. three strangers appear nearby. what do you do?
options: run to meet them and have a meal prepared.
nod politely and let them pass.
offer water from where you're sitting.
fork.reveal: Abraham runs, bows to the ground, and has bread baked and a calf prepared. Hebrews 13 looks back on afternoons like this one: some have entertained angels.

original.note: Greek: hospitality, literally love of strangers (Hebrews 13:2).

trapdoor: what you thought: be nice to strangers, because one might be an angel.
what it means: you can't sort people in advance, so welcome everyone, the way Abraham welcomed three strangers before he knew who they were.
what a scholar hears: philoxenia, love of the stranger, set right beside philadelphia, love of the brothers and sisters, in Hebrews 13:1–2.

604.title: Every best gift (James 1:17)
604.hook: every good gift comes from the Father of lights
604.howItsDone: Catholics give thanks for God's gifts in grace before meals, in the thanksgiving after Communion, and in the Mass itself, whose name Eucharist comes from the Greek for thanksgiving.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last chapter of Hebrews: welcome strangers. Your line was angels unawares. Whose name did you learn? Day six hundred four.

A sundial works only because the light keeps moving. Morning shadows stretch long to the west, shrink to almost nothing at noon, and swing around to the east by evening. The sun is faithful, but it never holds still, and everything it touches casts a shadow that turns. Winter days are short, summer days are long, clouds come and go. Today we open a new letter, the letter of James, and in its first chapter James looks up at that moving sky and says something about the one who made it.
screen: `A SUNDIAL NEEDS MOVING LIGHT.` → `EVERY SHADOW TURNS.` → `A NEW LETTER: JAMES.`

segments.voice: The letter opens simply: James, the servant of God and of the Lord Jesus Christ, to the twelve tribes scattered abroad. Which James? The letter doesn't say. Many in the early Church held it was James of Jerusalem, called the brother of the Lord, and Catholic tradition has often identified him with James the Less, one of the twelve. Scholars still discuss it. Then, almost at once, James talks about trials and temptation. And he draws a firm line. When someone is tempted, they shouldn't say God is tempting them. God tempts no one. Temptation grows from our own desires. So where does God come in? Here, in the Douay-Rheims: "Every best gift, and every perfect gift, is from above, coming down from the Father of lights, with whom there is no change, nor shadow of alteration." Father of lights. Many readers hear the lights of Genesis one here: the sun, the moon, the stars, which God made. Those lights move. They wax and wane, rise and set, and the shadows they cast turn all day long. God doesn't. With him, James says, there's no shadow of alteration. The good he gives isn't a passing mood that will swing around by evening. And the very next verse names the greatest gift: of his own will God has brought us to birth by the word of truth. Put it together and the line becomes a habit of attention. The good things in a life, the friend, the meal, the recovery, the morning, have a source, and James traces them up.
screen: `WHICH JAMES? THE LETTER DOESN'T SAY.` · `GOD TEMPTS NO ONE.` · `THE FATHER OF LIGHTS.` · `NO SHADOW OF ALTERATION.` · then, large: `EVERY BEST GIFT IS FROM ABOVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank God for one gift. Sit comfortably near a window if you can, and notice where the light is falling right now. Breathe. Then choose one good thing from the past day. Something specific: a conversation, a warm meal, a task that went right, a body that carried you around. Hold it in mind as if it had just been handed to you. Trace it up, step by step: who made it possible, and who made them possible. If you pray, you can thank God for it by name, the way James would trace it back to the Father of lights. If you don't, just let yourself be grateful. The bell holds the time.
Every best gift. James one seventeen: every good and perfect gift comes from above, from the Father of lights, who doesn't change. Today's word.
Your line: from above. Today, when something good happens, even something small, stop for one breath and say from above. Day six hundred four.

options: God is testing you on purpose.

fork.reveal: James draws the line firmly: God tempts no one. then he turns it around. what comes from God is every best gift.

what it means: James traces every good thing to God, who, unlike the shifting lights in the sky, doesn't change.
what a scholar hears: Father of lights, the maker of the heavenly bodies of Genesis 1. their shadows turn; with God there's no shadow of alteration.

605.title: Doers of the word (James 1:19–27)
605.hook: swift to hear, slow to speak, and not hearers only
605.howItsDone: At every Mass Catholics hear readings from scripture and a homily, and the Mass ends with a dismissal sending the people out; many parishes link the Sunday word to works of mercy such as visiting the sick, the elderly and the bereaved.

segments.voice: Yesterday, every best gift, coming down from the Father of lights. Your line was from above. What small good thing did you trace back up? Day six hundred five.

On your way out the door you catch yourself in the hall mirror. Hair sticking up. Something green in your teeth. You see it clearly. You even make a face at it. Then your keys are in your hand, the door shuts behind you, and by the time you reach the car the mirror is gone from your mind, and so is the spinach. Two hours later someone at work tells you. James knew that moment. Nineteen centuries before hall mirrors were cheap, he used it to describe the way people listen to God's word.
screen: `THE HALL MIRROR ON THE WAY OUT.` → `YOU SAW IT, THEN FORGOT.` → `JAMES KNEW THAT MOMENT.`

segments.voice: It starts with three speeds. The Douay-Rheims: "let every man be swift to hear, but slow to speak, and slow to anger." Fast ears, slow mouth, slower temper. Most arguments run the other way round. Then the line this whole passage turns on: "But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves." Deceiving yourselves. Hearing feels like progress. A good homily, a moving reading, a podcast that lands, and something in you says, there, that's done. James says that feeling can fool you. And here comes the mirror. Someone who hears the word and doesn't do it, he says, is like a man who looks at his own face in a glass, walks away, and forgets at once what he looked like. The word works like a mirror. It shows you yourself. The question is whether you do anything about what you saw. The Greek for doers is poietai, the word English later borrowed as poet. A poet is a maker. So a doer of the word is someone who makes something out of what they heard. Then James gets practical. Rein in your tongue. And he gives a short definition of religion that is hard to wriggle out of: religion that's pure in God's sight is this, "to visit the fatherless and widows in their tribulation," and to keep yourself unstained by the world. Not more listening. Visiting. Catholics hear the word at every Mass, and at the end of it the people are sent out: go. The hearing happens inside. The doing happens on the way home.
screen: `SWIFT TO HEAR, SLOW TO SPEAK.` · `HEARING CAN FOOL YOU.` · `THE MAN AT THE MIRROR FORGETS.` · `VISIT THE FATHERLESS AND WIDOWS.` · then, large: `BE YE DOERS OF THE WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do one thing you heard at Mass. Sit comfortably and breathe. Think back to the last Mass you went to, or, if that was a while ago, to any line of scripture you've heard this week. Let one phrase come back. Don't search for the best one; take the first that sticks. Then ask what it would look like on a Tuesday. A call to make. A visit. An apology. A meal for someone. Picture yourself doing it, today, specifically: where, when, the first words you'd say. If you pray, you can ask for the help to do it. If you don't, just choose it and hold it. The bell holds the time.
Doers of the word. James one: not hearers only, who see themselves in the mirror and forget, but makers, who do what they heard. Today's word.
Your line: doers, not hearers. Today, do the thing you chose before you go to bed, even in its smallest form. Day six hundred five.

fork.reveal: James says hearers only deceive themselves. and talking right away isn't it either: he wants people swift to hear and slow to speak.

trapdoor: what you thought: listen in church, then live your life.
what it means: hearing that doesn't turn into doing is like seeing your face in a mirror and forgetting it at once.

606.title: Faith without works (James 2:14–26)
606.hook: faith without works is dead; Catholics hold Paul and James together, and Christians have long discussed them
606.howItsDone: The Catholic Church teaches that justification is a free gift of grace received in faith, and that faith comes alive in charity; Catholics express this through the corporal and spiritual works of mercy, such as feeding the hungry, clothing the naked and visiting the sick.

segments.voice: Yesterday, doers of the word, and the man at the mirror who saw his face and forgot it. Your line was doers, not hearers. Did the thing you chose get done? Day six hundred six.

It's cold out. A man with no coat stops you on the sidewalk and says he hasn't eaten since yesterday. You smile, look him in the eye, and say, warmly: go in peace, stay warm, eat well. Then you walk on. You meant every word. You'd even pray for him later. James sets up exactly this scene in his second chapter, and then asks one blunt question. What good is that? It's one of the sharpest questions in the New Testament, and Christians have talked about what it means ever since.
screen: `A MAN WITH NO COAT.` → `GO IN PEACE, STAY WARM.` → `WHAT GOOD IS THAT?`

segments.voice: James's answer is famous. In the Douay-Rheims: "For even as the body without the spirit is dead; so also faith without works is dead." Faith that never moves is like a body with no breath in it. Then he pushes further. You believe there is one God? Good. "The devils also believe and tremble." Knowing the right things isn't the same as trusting God with your life. And he points to Abraham offering Isaac, and to Rahab, who hid the spies: their faith showed itself in what they did. Now the puzzle. Paul, writing to the Romans, says we are justified by faith, without the works of the law. James says, "Do you see that by works a man is justified; and not by faith only?" Are they arguing? Christians have discussed this for centuries, and they don't all answer the same way. Catholic teaching holds the two together. Salvation is a free gift of grace that nobody can earn; Paul is clear about that. And the faith that receives it is meant to come alive in love; James is clear about that. Paul himself puts both in one phrase in Galatians: "faith that worketh by charity." Many Protestant Christians read it this way: we are saved by faith alone, and living faith always produces good works, which is what James is describing. In nineteen ninety-nine, the Catholic Church and the Lutheran World Federation signed a joint declaration saying they share a basic understanding of justification, while naming the differences that remain. On a Tuesday, though, James's test is simple. Look at the man with no coat. Faith shows up as a coat.
screen: `A BODY WITH NO BREATH.` · `THE DEVILS ALSO BELIEVE.` · `PAUL AND JAMES HELD TOGETHER.` · `FAITH THAT WORKETH BY CHARITY.` · then, large: `FAITH WITHOUT WORKS IS DEAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pair belief with action. Sit comfortably and breathe. Name one thing you believe, quietly, in a sentence: that people matter, that God is generous, that the poor are close to God, that forgiveness is possible. Hold it for a moment. Then attach one small action to it, something you could actually do this week. If you believe people matter, maybe it's a call to someone lonely. If you believe in generosity, maybe it's giving something away. Let the belief and the action sit side by side, like a breath and a body. If you pray, you can offer them both to God. The bell holds the time.
Faith without works. James two: faith that never acts is like a body without breath. Today's word.
Your line: faith that works. Today, do the action you paired with your belief, or at least take its first step. Day six hundred six.

James never drops faith. he says faith that never acts is dead, like a body without breath.
Catholic teaching says people earn salvation by good works
the Church teaches salvation is a free gift of grace nobody can earn; faith comes alive in charity.
Catholics and Lutherans signed a joint declaration on justification in 1999

fork.setup: a man with no coat tells you he hasn't eaten since yesterday. you mean him well. what would James count as faith here?
options: a warm blessing: go in peace, stay warm, eat well.
a promise to pray for him later.
giving him what his body needs.
fork.reveal: James sets up this very scene and asks: if you don't give them what the body needs, what good is it? prayer matters, but faith shows up as a coat.

original.note: Greek: works, deeds (James 2:26). the same root gives English energy and ergonomic.

trapdoor: what you thought: James and Paul flatly disagree about faith.
what it means: Catholic teaching holds them together: salvation is a free gift, and the faith that receives it comes alive in love.
what a scholar hears: Paul argues against relying on the works of the law; James against a faith that only assents. in 1999 Catholics and Lutherans signed a joint declaration on justification.

sources.ref: Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification (1999); Catechism of the Catholic Church 1987–2011

607.title: Is any man sick (James 5:13–16)
607.hook: call the priests to anoint the sick: the Church's root for anointing
607.howItsDone: In the sacrament of the Anointing of the Sick, a priest prays over a seriously ill or elderly person, lays hands on them in silence and anoints their forehead and hands with oil blessed by the bishop; families can ask their parish or a hospital chaplain for it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, faith without works: a body with no breath. Your line was faith that works. Which belief got its action? Day six hundred seven.

Many parish priests carry a small metal case, about the size of a lipstick, with a screw-top lid. Inside is a bit of cotton soaked in olive oil, blessed by the bishop during Holy Week. It rides in a coat pocket or a car glove box for months. Then one night the phone rings: a hospital, a nursing home, a kitchen where someone's father has taken a turn. The priest drives over, takes out the little case, and does something Christians have done since the first century. The instructions come from the end of the letter of James.
screen: `A SMALL METAL CASE OF OIL.` → `THE PHONE RINGS AT NIGHT.` → `INSTRUCTIONS FROM JAMES.`

segments.voice: James is wrapping up his letter, and he covers the whole range of life in three quick questions. Is anyone sad? Let him pray. Is anyone cheerful? Let him sing. And then, in the Douay-Rheims: "Is any man sick among you? Let him bring in the priests of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord." Notice who moves first. The sick person calls. Nobody is meant to suffer quietly in a back room so as not to be a bother. James goes on: "And the prayer of faith shall save the sick man: and the Lord shall raise him up: and if he be in sins, they shall be forgiven him." The Greek word for those priests is presbyteroi, elders, and our English word priest grows out of it. The Catholic Church sees in these verses the root of a sacrament, the Anointing of the Sick. The Council of Trent taught that it was hinted at in Mark's Gospel, where the twelve anointed many sick people with oil, and made known by James. For centuries it was mostly given at the very end of life and called Extreme Unction, the last anointing. After the Second Vatican Council the Church stressed its older name and wider use: anyone seriously ill, someone facing major surgery, the frail elderly, and it can be received more than once. The priest lays his hands on the person in silence, then anoints the forehead and the hands. The Church doesn't promise a cure. It speaks of strength, peace and courage, and of bodily healing too, if God wills it. Saved and raised up can mean more than one thing.
screen: `SAD? PRAY. CHEERFUL? SING.` · `THE SICK PERSON CALLS.` · `PRESBYTEROI: THE ELDERS.` · `FROM LAST RITES TO ANOINTING OF THE SICK.` · then, large: `THE PRAYER OF FAITH SHALL SAVE THE SICK MAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for someone sick, or hold them in mind. Sit comfortably and breathe slowly. Bring to mind one person who is ill right now: in the hospital, at home, or carrying something no one can see. Picture them as clearly as you can, where they are, how they're sitting or lying. If it feels right, imagine your hand resting gently on their shoulder. If you pray, you can pray for them by name, in your own words or with a prayer you know. If you don't, just stay with them in your thoughts and wish them strength and peace. The bell holds the time.
Is any man sick. James five: call the priests of the church to pray over the sick and anoint them. For Catholics, the root of the Anointing of the Sick. Today's word.
Your line: the prayer of faith. Today, let the person you held in mind know they're thought of: a message, a call, a visit. Day six hundred seven.

elders: root of the word priest

608.title: A living hope (1 Peter 1:3–9)
608.hook: born again into a living hope through the resurrection
608.howItsDone: Readings from the first letter of Peter are heard at Mass during the Easter season, and Catholics count hope as one of the three theological virtues, with faith and charity, anchored in the resurrection of Christ.

segments.voice: Yesterday, James and the oil of the sick. Your line was the prayer of faith. Who did you let know they were held in mind? Day six hundred eight.

The last time we saw Peter in the Gospels near a fire, he was warming his hands in a courtyard and swearing he had never met Jesus. Three times. Then a rooster crowed, and he went out and wept. Now picture the same man years later, a leader of the Church, writing to Christians scattered across what is now Turkey, people being mocked and pushed to the edges for their faith. He could open with anything. A warning. A plan. A word about his own failures. Instead, after a short greeting, the first thing out of his pen is a blessing, and the blessing is about hope.
screen: `PETER BY THE COURTYARD FIRE.` → `YEARS LATER, A LETTER.` → `IT OPENS WITH HOPE.`

segments.voice: Here it is in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy hath regenerated us unto a lively hope, by the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead." Lively. In older English that word meant living. The Greek says it plainly: a living hope. Not a wish. Not optimism, which is a weather forecast about how things will probably turn out. Peter's hope is anchored in something that already happened: a tomb that was empty, a friend he saw alive again. And he had more reason than most to need it. The one who denied Jesus was the one Jesus came back for. Then Peter describes what the hope looks toward, an inheritance with three nots. It can't perish. It can't be stained. It can't fade. In Greek all three start with the same little a-, meaning not, and the last one, amarantos, unfading, gave its name to the amaranth, a flower people once believed never withered. Peter doesn't pretend the present is easy. He says his readers are grieving in various trials for a while, and he compares their faith to gold tested by fire. The hope doesn't remove the fire. It tells you what the fire is for. Then one of the tenderest lines in his letter: "Whom having not seen, you love." Peter had seen. They hadn't. He's writing to people like almost every Christian since, who love someone they've never laid eyes on, and he tells them that their joy is real anyway.
screen: `LIVELY MEANS LIVING.` · `HOPE, NOT A WEATHER FORECAST.` · `CAN'T PERISH, STAIN OR FADE.` · `WHOM HAVING NOT SEEN, YOU LOVE.` · then, large: `REGENERATED UNTO A LIVELY HOPE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name one hope. Sit comfortably and let your breathing settle. Notice what you're carrying right now, the trial, the worry, whatever's heavy. You don't need to fix it. Just let it be there. Then, underneath it, look for one hope. Not a forecast, not a plan. Something you hope for that's bigger than this week: for someone you love, for the world, for yourself. Name it once, quietly. If you pray, you can hold it alongside Peter's living hope, the resurrection. If you don't, just let the hope sit beside the weight, both of them real. The bell holds the time.
A living hope. First Peter one: a hope born of the resurrection, not a forecast but a life. Today's word.
Your line: a living hope. Today, when the worry comes back, name your hope right after it, out loud if you can. Day six hundred eight.

fork.setup: you're Peter, the one who denied Jesus three times. years later you write to Christians who are being mocked for their faith. how do you begin?
options: with an apology for your own failures.
with a blessing for the living hope of the resurrection.
with a warning about what's coming.
fork.reveal: after a short greeting, Peter blesses God for a living hope, born of the resurrection. the one who denied Jesus is the one Jesus came back for.

original.note: Greek: a living hope (1 Peter 1:3). the Douay-Rheims renders it a lively hope.

trapdoor: what you thought: hope means feeling optimistic about the future.
what it means: a living hope anchored in the resurrection, something already done, not a forecast of what might happen.
what a scholar hears: an inheritance aphthartos, amiantos, amarantos: three 'nots' in a row, and amarantos, unfading, named the amaranth flower.

609.title: A royal priesthood (1 Peter 2:9)
609.hook: every baptized person shares Christ's priesthood (CCC 1268)
609.howItsDone: Catholics are anointed with chrism at baptism as sharers in Christ's role as priest, prophet and king, and many pray a Morning Offering each day, giving God their prayers, works, joys and sufferings; the Church distinguishes this common priesthood of all the baptized from the ordained priesthood.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Peter by the fire, years later writing about hope. Your line was a living hope. Did you name your hope when the worry came back? Day six hundred nine.

At a Catholic baptism, just after the water, the priest takes a small vessel of perfumed oil called chrism and anoints the crown of the baby's head. Most guests are busy with their phones by then, and the baby is usually busy crying. But the prayer said over that moment is startling. It says this child is now joined to Christ, who was anointed priest, prophet and king. A priest. A newborn who can't yet hold up her own head. The idea comes straight out of today's verse.
screen: `OIL ON A BABY'S HEAD.` → `PRIEST, PROPHET AND KING.` → `STRAIGHT OUT OF TODAY'S VERSE.`

segments.voice: Peter is writing to ordinary people: slaves, wives, laborers, converts with no standing in their towns. And he tells them who they are. In the Douay-Rheims: "But you are a chosen generation, a kingly priesthood, a holy nation, a purchased people." Every phrase is borrowed. At Mount Sinai, in the book of Exodus, God told Israel they would be a priestly kingdom and a holy nation. Peter takes those old titles and gives them to these scattered Christians, without taking them away from anyone. A few verses earlier he says what a priest does. They are living stones, built into a spiritual house, a holy priesthood, offering spiritual sacrifices. So what does a priest do? Stands between God and the world, and offers things up. The Catechism puts it plainly: every baptized person shares in the priesthood of Christ. The Church calls this the common priesthood of the faithful. It also teaches that the ordained priesthood is different, not just a higher level of the same thing, but a distinct gift for serving the whole people, especially at the altar. Both are real. Neither replaces the other. So what does the common priesthood look like on a Thursday? Paul gives a hint in Romans: "present your bodies a living sacrifice." The sacrifice is the day itself. The commute, the spreadsheet, the diaper, the hospital shift, the patience with a difficult relative, offered to God. Many Catholics begin each morning with a traditional prayer called the Morning Offering, giving God the prayers, works, joys and sufferings of the day ahead. A whole day, held up like bread at the altar.
screen: `OLD TITLES FROM SINAI.` · `LIVING STONES, SPIRITUAL SACRIFICES.` · `COMMON AND ORDAINED PRIESTHOOD.` · `THE DAY ITSELF, OFFERED UP.` · then, large: `A KINGLY PRIESTHOOD, A HOLY NATION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: offer your day as a priest would. Sit comfortably and breathe. Walk through what's left of today, or what tomorrow holds: the work, the people, the chores, the thing you're dreading. Picture each one briefly. Then imagine gathering them all up in your hands, the good parts and the dull parts together, and lifting them, the way a priest lifts the bread at Mass. If you pray, you can offer them to God in your own words, or with the Morning Offering if you know it. If you don't, just hold the day up and look at it with care. The bell holds the time.
A royal priesthood. First Peter two nine: every baptized person shares in Christ's priesthood, offering up their life. Today's word.

Your line: a royal priesthood. Today, pick one ordinary task and do it as an offering, carefully, start to finish. And that's week eighty-seven: angels unawares, from above, doers not hearers, faith that works, the prayer of faith, a living hope, and a royal priesthood. Day six hundred nine.
